funding_pct: up to 85% of approved project expenses

criteria.details: Israeli individuals at the idea/concept stage (pre-incorporation is fine) or early-stage, pre-revenue startups with little to no external funding. Small or single-founder teams are explicitly accommodated -- team capability is still evaluated, but limited team size alone is not disqualifying.
criteria.common_mistake: Assuming any founder or team stage qualifies. Tnufa targets the earliest, pre-revenue, often pre-incorporation stage specifically -- a company already generating revenue or with a formal track record reads as too late-stage.

criteria.details: Broad eligibility across IT/software/cyber, healthcare and biotech, cleantech, agritech, advanced manufacturing, and defense/security tech, with a preference for disruptive, deep-tech innovation.
criteria.common_mistake: Believing only flashy 'high-tech' software projects get approved. This is a named misconception in the source material -- deep-tech, medical devices, agri-tech and other sectors are explicitly welcome.

criteria.details: Prototype development, technological feasibility studies, IP protection costs (patent filings), and early market validation -- but the market validation must be directly tied to proving the technology's viability, not a general go-to-market plan.
criteria.common_mistake: Padding the budget with general business expenses (office rent, general salaries, broad business-strategy consulting) or market work that is not tied to validating the technology itself -- Tnufa does not fund either.

criteria.details: Revenue-generating companies, projects that already secured substantial private or public funding, non-technological / pure business-model projects, and duplicate submissions of the same project across multiple Israel Innovation Authority tracks.
criteria.common_mistake: Applying while already generating meaningful revenue or holding substantial outside funding, or submitting the same project to more than one IIA track at once.

criteria.details: Up to 85% of approved project expenses, capped at roughly NIS 200,000 per project per year, over a 12-month program. Non-dilutive -- no equity changes hands.
criteria.common_mistake: The source FAQ contradicts itself here (one entry says 15-25% matching, another says a 50/50 match). The IIA Grants table resolves it: an 85%-of-costs grant implies roughly 15% matching, not 50/50 -- the 50/50 figure is stray residue from how the source doc was originally generated and should not be used.

criteria.aspect: Is Tnufa actually the right program
criteria.details: Best fit when: the project is at the earliest development stage, the funding need is primarily technical R&D (not operating costs), the applicant is prepared for a multi-stage evaluation process, and there is a credible plan for what happens after the 12-month grant (angel, VC, or a later-stage IIA track).
criteria.common_mistake: Applying when the real need is operational/business funding rather than technical R&D, or having no articulated plan for funding beyond the Tnufa period.

criteria.aspect: How the application is actually submitted
criteria.details: Submitted online through the Israel Innovation Authority portal with a project description, team information, a work plan, and a budget, all attached and complete at submission.
criteria.common_mistake: Missing a required document or section at submission -- this alone commonly delays or disqualifies an otherwise strong application at the administrative-review stage.

criteria.details: A staged review: an administrative completeness check first, then a technical and financial assessment by subject-matter experts, then a committee decision.
criteria.common_mistake: Writing the technological-innovation explanation for a specialist audience only. Reviewers span technical, business, and financial backgrounds, so an explanation that only a deep specialist can follow reads as unclear, not impressive.

criteria.details: States the problem clearly, explains how the technology solves it, and is explicit about what is actually novel about the approach versus existing alternatives.
criteria.common_mistake: A vague description that asserts innovation without naming what specifically is new, or an unclear timeline for what gets built during the grant period.

criteria.details: Presents the team's relevant technical and industry expertise, and for a small or single-founder team, explicitly addresses how expertise gaps will be covered (advisors, planned hires, contractors).
criteria.common_mistake: A small team with no stated plan for covering an obvious expertise gap (e.g. a deep-tech project with no technical co-founder and no named advisor).

criteria.details: A milestone-based plan across the 12-month period with concrete deliverables (a working prototype, a completed feasibility test, a technical validation result).
criteria.common_mistake: Milestones stated too vaguely to be checked against later, or a timeline that is not realistic for a 12-month, R&D-focused grant.

criteria.details: An itemized, realistic budget tied line-by-line to the work plan, focused on R&D costs (materials, lab or testing time, IP filing fees) rather than general operating costs.
criteria.common_mistake: A budget built without real research behind it (round-number guessing), or budget lines for costs Tnufa does not fund (office rent, general salaries, generic business consulting).

criteria.details: Early market-validation evidence is welcome (surveys, letters of interest, competitor analysis) as long as it is framed as evidence the TECHNOLOGY has real demand, not as a general business plan.
criteria.common_mistake: Treating the market-validation section as a general go-to-market pitch, or asserting demand without any supporting evidence.

criteria.details: A registered Israeli entity (or documented pre-incorporation individual-applicant status where applicable), with IP-ownership agreements formalized in writing among all founders/team members before applying.
criteria.common_mistake: Incomplete company registration, or no written IP-ownership agreement among team members -- a common source of dispute once funding arrives.

criteria.aspect: Using the grant for IP protection
criteria.details: Grant funds may legitimately cover patent-filing and other IP-legal costs; the applicant retains IP ownership but must disclose IP developments to the Israel Innovation Authority during the grant period.
criteria.common_mistake: Not budgeting for IP protection at all, despite it being an explicitly eligible and often underused use of the grant.

criteria.details: The applicant must be able to demonstrate the roughly 15% matching contribution (personal funds or another funding source) before final approval and disbursement.
criteria.common_mistake: No clear, demonstrable source for the matching funds at application time -- a common reason for delay or rejection at the funding-proof stage.

criteria.details: Periodic technical and financial progress reports against the stated milestones and budget, submitted on the schedule set in the grant agreement.
criteria.common_mistake: Treating reporting as a formality. Missing or incomplete reports can pause or cancel further fund disbursement.

criteria.aspect: Changing scope, budget, or team after approval
criteria.details: Material changes to project scope, budget allocation, or key team members after approval require a formal written request and Israel Innovation Authority approval before proceeding.
criteria.common_mistake: Making an unapproved change to scope, budget, or a key team member's role after the grant is awarded -- this can trigger penalties or a clawback of funds.
